Most trading systems don't fail because of strategy. They fail because of architecture.

So how do you feed 30+ independent trading strategies from a single market data connection without letting any strategy block, slow down, or crash another?

This document is my answer.

I've been designing and building a production-grade Multi-Strategy Trading System. While most discussions in algorithmic trading focus on alpha, signals, or execution, I wanted to solve a different problem:

How do you build an infrastructure that remains fast, reliable, and scalable as the number of strategies grows?

This PDF is not about trading logic or performance metrics. Instead, it focuses on the engineering principles that make a complex trading platform stable in production. 

Inside this document, you'll find:

• How 30+ independent strategy processes share a single market data connection without interfering with each other.

• Why I chose a shared-memory tick bus instead of Redis, databases, or traditional message queues for market data.

• How ZeroMQ PUB/SUB enables clean, scalable communication between strategies and multiple execution accounts.

• The role of process isolation in preventing one strategy from slowing down or crashing the rest of the system.

• How execution adapters, observability, logging, and deployment were designed to keep the system reliable and easy to operate. 

One idea completely changed how I approached this architecture:

| "Tick data is not a stream to consume. It is a value to look up." |

That simple shift transformed a messaging problem into a shared-state problem and ultimately shaped the entire system architecture. 

I hope this document is useful for engineers working on low-latency systems, distributed architectures, quantitative trading platforms, or any software where performance, isolation, and scalability matter.

I'm always happy to discuss ideas, exchange feedback, and learn from others building similar systems.

1. What this system does This is the architecture of a production intraday index options trading system that I designed and built. The system solves one specific problem: Run many independent trading strategies simultaneously, feed all of them from one market data connection, and route every resulting signal to multiple execution accounts — without any strategy ever being able to slow down, block, or crash another. That single constraint drove every architectural decision that follows. The result is a system where roughly 40 processes run concurrently on a single machine, sharing market data through memory rather than the network, and communicating through a message bus rather than function calls. 2. The core design problem A naive multi-strategy system is a single process with a loop: for strategy in strategies: strategy.on_tick(tick) This breaks down fast, in three ways. One slow strategy blocks all of them. If one strategy does a heavy numerical calculation on a tick, every other strategy waits. In a market where entries are timed to the second, that is unacceptable. One crash kills all of them. An unhandled exception in any strategy takes down the entire process — including strategies that currently hold open positions. Deployment becomes all-or-nothing. You cannot restart, patch, or add a strategy without stopping everything. Multi-Strategy Trading System —Architecture 4

The alternative — one process per strategy — solves all three, but creates a new problem: how do 30+ separate processes read the same market data without each opening its own connection? That question is where the interesting engineering lives. 3.
